title: U.S. Senate · West Virginia
area: The entire state of West Virginia.

context.text: Incumbent Shelley Moore Capito (R) won the Republican primary on May 12, 2026 with 66.5% of the vote. Rachel Fetty Anderson defeated Jeffrey Kessler, Zachary Shrewsbury, Thornton Cooper, and Rio Phillips in the Democratic primary with 33.2% of the vote.

candidates.name: Shelley Moore Capito
candidates.ballotNote: Won the May 12 Republican primary with 66.5% of the vote

summary.text: Shelley Moore Capito is the incumbent Republican U.S. Senator from West Virginia, seeking a third term in 2026. A former college counselor and state delegate, she served in the U.S. House from 2001 to 2015 before her election to the Senate in 2014. She chairs the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.

background.text: Born Shelley Moore in Glen Dale, West Virginia, in 1953, the daughter of former Gov. Arch A. Moore Jr.
Earned a bachelor's degree from Duke University and a master's degree in education from the University of Virginia.
Worked as a college counselor and then director of an educational information center before entering politics.
Served in the West Virginia House of Delegates before her election to Congress.

Elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2000 and served from 2001 to 2015. She was the first Republican woman elected to Congress from West Virginia, and founded the Congressional Coal Caucus after an explosion that killed 29 coal workers; she is a former chairwoman of the Congressional Caucus for Women's Issues.
Elected to the U.S. Senate in 2014, becoming the first woman elected to the Senate from West Virginia, and re-elected in 2020, defeating Democrat Paula Jean Swearengin.

Chairs the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (2025-2026) and sits on the Commerce, Science, and Transportation; Appropriations; and Rules and Administration committees. She chairs the Appropriations subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies.
Married to Charles Capito; they have three children.

record.text: Chairs the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works for the 119th Congress (2025-2026), and serves on the Senate Committee on Appropriations and the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

candidates.name: Rachel Fetty Anderson
candidates.ballotNote: Won the May 12 Democratic primary with 33.2% of the vote

summary.text: Rachel Fetty Anderson is a public interest attorney running as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate from West Virginia. She describes her work representing children, families, and individuals, and her campaign website lists priorities including health care, children and families, and human rights.

background.text: Was homeschooled and earned a GED.
Earned a bachelor's degree from Iowa State University in 1996 and a law degree from the University of Iowa in 1999.
Works as a public interest attorney; says she has represented children, families, and individuals, and has seen the foster care system from both sides.
Describes herself as a mother of four whose family has lived in West Virginia since 2007.

priorities.text: "I am committed to improving the health, safety and environment of our people and our children."
"HUMAN RIGHTS: Your humanity is enough... we will afford you access to the processes, protections, resources and rights granted to you by the law."

positions.summary: Says pregnant people are entitled to autonomous decision-making over their bodies, including the right to choose or refuse medical care.
positions.quote: All adult humans have the same human rights regardless of the nature of their reproductive capacity including the right to appropriate educational services, autonomous decision making over their bodies, to choose or refuse medical care, including birth control, to choose their providers and to exercise their rights to privacy.

positions.summary: Supports raising the marginal tax rate on income over $500,000 per year.
positions.quote: I support the elimination of the "Buy, Borrow, Die" tax loop-hole, the increase of the marginal tax rate of earners of over $500,000.00 per year.

candidates.name: S. Marshall Wilson
candidates.currentRole: Former member, West Virginia House of Delegates

summary.text: S. Marshall Wilson is a former West Virginia state delegate running as the Constitution Party nominee for U.S. Senate. He is a U.S. Army veteran, former missionary and teacher who served in the House of Delegates from 2016 to 2020 and has since run statewide as a third-party and write-in candidate.

background.text: Born in Beaufort, South Carolina; served in the U.S. Army.
Graduated from Louisiana State University and earned an executive master of arts in national security affairs from the Institute of World Politics in Washington, D.C.
Worked as a missionary to Peru and as a teacher at Liberty University.

Represented District 60 in the West Virginia House of Delegates from 2016 to 2020, serving on committees including House Judiciary and House Health and Human Resources. He was elected as a Republican, unopposed in 2018, and did not run for re-election in 2020.
Changed his party registration from Republican to independent on December 17, 2019, citing a dispute with the state Republican Party chair.

Ran for Governor of West Virginia in 2020 as a write-in independent (about 1.9% of the vote) and in 2024 as the Constitution Party candidate (about 2.3%); lost a 2022 House of Delegates race in District 91 as the Constitution Party candidate.

priorities.text: Campaign website material emphasizes constitutional government and states that the purpose of West Virginia's government must follow the U.S. Constitution as "the supreme Law of the Land."

positions.summary: As a West Virginia state delegate, voted yes on SJR 12, a constitutional amendment stating that nothing in the West Virginia Constitution protects a right to abortion or requires public funding of abortion; the House adopted it 73-26 on March 5, 2018, and voters approved it as Amendment 1 that November.

record.text: Voted yes on SJR 12 (a constitutional amendment stating the West Virginia Constitution does not protect a right to abortion or require public funding of abortion), which the House of Delegates adopted 73-26 on March 5, 2018.
